hook_text: For thirty years, the ANC wrote polite letters to the government, and then a group of young people said: enough.
clip_script: 1912. The ANC is born. Its leaders are teachers, lawyers and writers. They write petitions. They sail to Britain to ask for help. The answer is always no. And the laws get worse. 1944. A group of young members forms the Youth League: Lembede, Sisulu, Tambo, Mandela. Their message: stop asking. Start acting. In 1949, the ANC adopts their Programme of Action. Boycotts. Strikes. Civil disobedience. No violence, but no cooperation either. The government strikes back. In 1950, the Suppression of Communism Act bans the Communist Party, and defines communism so widely that almost anyone who opposes apartheid can be silenced without a trial. The 1950s will be a decade of growing resistance, met at every step by growing repression.
visual_style: Old photographs of the 1912 founders in suits; a typed petition; young Youth League members in the 1940s; a crowd at a 1950 protest meeting; a newspaper headline about the Suppression of Communism Act; a banning order document stamped by the Minister of Justice.
pacing: Slow at the petitions, quickening at the Youth League, firm at the ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how resistance to apartheid changed at the start of the 1950s.
